questions.question: What does the Command pattern encapsulate?
options: A reference to a singleton manager
A request or action as an object that can be stored, passed, and executed later
A way to create objects without specifying their class
A method for iterating over collections
questions.explanation: The Command pattern wraps an action (with its parameters) in an object. This lets you queue commands, undo them, replay them, or rebind inputs — because the invoker doesn't need to know what the command actually does.
questions.hint: Think about undo/redo — how would you store an action to reverse it later?

questions.question: How does the Command pattern enable an undo system?
options: By storing a reference to the previous scene
Each command object has an Execute and an Undo method that reverses the action
By saving the entire game state every frame
By using Time.timeScale to rewind
questions.explanation: Each command knows how to do and undo itself. You push executed commands onto a stack. To undo, pop the last command and call its Undo method. To redo, call Execute again.
questions.hint: Each command needs to know both what it does and how to reverse it.

questions.question: What problem does the State pattern solve?
options: Managing object pooling
Replacing complex if/switch chains by delegating behaviour to state objects
Sorting collections efficiently
Sharing data between scenes
questions.explanation: Instead of a growing switch statement checking which state you're in, each state is its own object with its own behaviour. The main object delegates to the current state object, and switching states means swapping which object it delegates to.

questions.question: In a finite state machine (FSM), what determines when a transition occurs?
options: The game loop forces transitions every frame
Conditions defined in each state trigger transitions to other states
States transition in a fixed order that never changes
The garbage collector triggers transitions
questions.explanation: Each state defines its own transition logic — for example, an enemy in Patrol state transitions to Chase when the player enters detection range. The conditions are checked within the state itself.
questions.hint: Think about enemy AI: what makes a patrolling enemy start chasing?

questions.question: What does the Factory pattern do?
options: Destroys objects when they are no longer needed
Centralises object creation so the caller doesn't need to know the concrete class
Prevents more than one instance from being created
Serialises objects to disk
questions.explanation: A Factory method or class handles the creation of objects. The caller asks for an object through an interface without knowing which concrete class is instantiated. This makes it easy to add new types without changing calling code.

questions.question: How can the Factory pattern be combined with Object Pool?
options: The factory always creates new instances and the pool destroys them
The factory returns recycled objects from the pool instead of always instantiating new ones
Object Pool replaces Factory entirely
They cannot be combined
questions.explanation: The factory becomes a recycling plant — callers still ask it for objects, but internally it checks the pool first. If a deactivated object is available, it returns that instead of instantiating a new one.

questions.question: What does the Flyweight pattern achieve?
options: It makes objects move faster
It reduces memory usage by sharing common data across many instances
It creates lightweight threads for each object
It compresses object data on disk
questions.explanation: Flyweight separates shared (intrinsic) data from per-instance (extrinsic) data. A thousand soldiers can share one mesh, texture, and animation set — each soldier only stores its own position and health. Unity's sharedMaterial and sharedMesh are implementations of this pattern.
questions.hint: In a strategy game with 1000 identical soldiers, what data is the same for all of them?

questions.question: Which Unity feature is an implementation of the Flyweight pattern?
options: DontDestroyOnLoad
ScriptableObjects used as shared data containers
Coroutines
Physics.Raycast
questions.explanation: When multiple objects reference the same ScriptableObject for shared configuration data, that's Flyweight — the shared data lives in one asset, and each instance only holds its own unique state. Unity's sharedMaterial works the same way.

questions.question: What problem does the Event Queue pattern solve compared to the Observer pattern?
options: Event Queue removes the need for events entirely
Event Queue spreads event processing over multiple frames to avoid freezing when many events fire at once
Event Queue makes events type-safe
Event Queue prevents memory leaks from unsubscribed listeners
questions.explanation: With Observer, all subscribers execute immediately when an event fires. If 100 enemies die at once, 100 death handlers run in the same frame. Event Queue buffers events and processes them over time, preventing frame spikes.
questions.hint: What happens if the Observer triggers 50 methods in a single frame?

questions.question: How does the Service Locator pattern differ from a Singleton?
options: Service Locator is faster than Singleton
Service Locator provides access to a service through an abstraction, allowing the implementation to be swapped
There is no meaningful difference
Service Locator can only be used with static classes
questions.explanation: Both provide global access, but Service Locator returns a service behind an interface. You can swap the implementation (e.g. real audio vs null audio for testing) without changing any calling code. A Singleton hardcodes the concrete class.
questions.hint: What if you want to swap real audio for a silent mock during testing?

questions.question: What is the core idea behind the Component pattern?
options: All logic should live in a single manager class
Break behaviour into independent, reusable pieces that can be attached to any object
Components must always communicate with each other
Each GameObject should have exactly one component
questions.explanation: The Component pattern decouples functionality into self-contained pieces. In Unity, this is the entire architecture — you attach Rigidbody, Collider, and your own scripts independently to any GameObject.

questions.question: What does the Decorator pattern allow you to do?
options: Remove behaviour from an object permanently
Add behaviour to an individual object at runtime without modifying its class
Replace inheritance entirely
Create copies of an object
questions.explanation: Decorators wrap an object and add behaviour on top of it. A weapon can be wrapped with a SilencerDecorator, then a ScopeDecorator — each adds functionality without modifying the base weapon class. Decorators can be stacked and removed at runtime.
questions.hint: Think about attaching a silencer and a scope to a weapon — each modifies the weapon's behaviour independently.

questions.question: What does the Facade pattern provide?
options: A way to duplicate objects
A simplified interface to a complex subsystem of classes
A method for saving game state
An event-driven messaging system
questions.explanation: A Facade is a single class that provides a simple interface to a complex group of classes. Instead of interacting with 10 audio classes directly, you interact with an AudioManager facade that exposes PlaySound, StopAll, etc.

questions.question: Why does the Double Buffer pattern use two buffers instead of one?
options: To use more memory for better performance
So one buffer can be read from while the other is being written to, preventing partial or corrupted data
To compress data more efficiently
To allow multithreaded access without locks
questions.explanation: With one buffer, readers would see partially updated data. Double Buffer lets you write a complete new frame to buffer A while buffer B displays the previous frame. When writing is done, you swap them. This is how screen rendering, cellular automata, and motion blur work.
questions.hint: What would happen if you read from the same buffer you're writing to?
